data_scope.spatial_coverage: United States, employer-sponsored insurance enrollees; individuals geolocated at 3-digit ZIP level mapped to dominant county FIPS; census region and urbanization tertile derived (number of distinct ZIP3s/counties not reported)
data_scope.source_database_size: approximately 200 million unique covered lives in MarketScan CCAE
data_scope.screening_funnel: 66,054,423 family identifiers with >=1 candidate member; 27,975,854 families with >=2 valid candidate children
data_scope.eligibility: >=365 days enrollment visibility and age at last observation >=12 years per child; exactly two non-parent children per family
data_scope.data_availability: individual-level MarketScan data are proprietary and licensed (data use agreement with Merative required); summary-level results in Supplementary Tables 1-15 and source data; analysis code open at github.com/benjaminkramer510/BirthOrderPhenome2026

core_conclusion: Birth order is associated with disease risk across nearly the entire clinical phenome rather than only the few conditions studied previously. Scanning 569 ICD-defined diseases in 10.27 million siblings from 5.13 million two-child US claims families, 150 of 418 testable diseases reach Bonferroni significance: first-borns carry excess risk for neurodevelopmental and immune-allergic conditions (other/unspecified PDD code group OR = 0.57, autism OR = 0.74, food allergy OR = 0.80), second-borns for substance abuse (OR = 1.19), gastrointestinal and infectious conditions (herpes zoster OR = 1.35). A high-powered between-family matched scan and an internally controlled within-family sibling contrast agree (r = 0.66; 84.7% of significant hits directionally concordant), and results survive state fixed effects (r > 0.99), full-sibling restriction, stricter clinical rematching (r = 0.93) and healthcare-use adjustment (r = 0.99), though individual effect sizes are modest (median OR about 0.89 for first-born excess and 1.10 for second-born excess).
why_it_matters: Converts a century of fragmented, disease-by-disease birth-order research into a single comparable atlas across organ systems; birth order is a universal exposure, so modest ORs translate into nontrivial population-level burden and screening-prioritization value; the dual between-/within-family design with prespecified positive and negative controls offers a reusable template for any non-randomizable familial exposure; and it directly tests rather than assumes away reproductive stoppage, differential healthcare use, parental-age and age-period-cohort confounding.
why_nature: Reframes a whole field rather than adding one estimate (569 phenotypes at once); population-health scale (10.27 million individuals) anchored in real-world clinical diagnoses; methodological rigour is itself the contribution (dual-design triangulation, prespecified controls, empirical-Bayes domain pooling, seven robustness specifications); calibrated causal claims with explicit limits on the employer-insured sampling frame; and a resource contribution via disease-level supplementary catalogues plus fully open analysis code.
